papers.title_in_file: Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks are Effectively Classically Simulable
papers.version_note: arXiv:2408.12739v2 [quant-ph], dated 20 Feb 2026; the text layer holds the paper once. The record id carries 2026 and the file name carries 2024, which matches the v1 date of the preprint and this v2 text.
papers.what_it_is: A preprint arguing, with a classical surrogate built from Pauli propagation, tensor networks and classical shadows, that tracing out and measurement-based QCNNs are effectively classically simulable on the locally-easy benchmark datasets used in the literature.

existing.note: The 1024 qubit size applies only to the XXX bond-alternating task; the Haldane chain is 512 qubits, the ANNNI and cluster tasks are 32 qubits and the classical image tasks are simulated on 8 qubits. The comparison baseline is accuracy reported in the literature for full QCNNs, not a QCNN the authors ran. Classical-dataset accuracies are the best of 5 runs. The surrogate is trained to solve the task, not to emulate the training of an exact QCNN.
existing.value: The authors report that the classical surrogate matches or outperforms standard QCNNs on the benchmark datasets, with 1024 qubits for the XXX chain, 512 qubits for the Haldane chain, 32 qubits for the ANNNI and cluster models and 8 qubits for the classical image datasets, compared against accuracies reported in the literature for full QCNNs, and with the classical-dataset results given as the best of 5 runs.

existing.value: The authors state that there is currently no evidence that QCNNs will work on classically non-trivial tasks, and that their exhaustive literature search did not produce a single example of a task that cannot be classified by simulating the QCNN in the low-bodyness subspace.

our exhaustive literature search did not produce a single example of a task that cannot be classified by simulating the action of the QCNN in the small subspace of low-bodyness observables
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the search protocol is not described.
existing.reader_inference: The paper gives no search protocol, so the exhaustive literature search cannot be checked from the text.

existing.value: The authors state that their work does not intend to prove that no scenario needs a QCNN trained on a quantum computer, that the burden of proof now rests on proponents of QCNNs, and that their claims do not amount to a full dequantization of QCNNs.
quotes: Clearly, our work cannot, and does not intend to, prove that there is no scenario whatsoever where it may be necessary to train a QCNN on a quantum computer.
the burden of proof now rests firmly in the hands of any proponent of QCNNs
our claims do not amount to a full dequantization of QCNNs
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and limits of its own claims in Section V.
existing.reader_inference: Section V adds the reason: at least for quantum input data, a quantum computer is needed to obtain classical shadows.

assertions.value: The authors define a dataset for a supervised QML classification task as locally-easy if it can be classified using the expectation values of low-bodyness observables of the input quantum states.
quotes: Definition 1 (Locally-easy dataset). Given a dataset for a supervised QML classification task, we will say that it is locally-easy if it can be classified using the expectation values of low-bodyness observables of the input quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 1 in Section III.B.
assertions.reader_inference: The definition does not fix how low the bodyness must be or what accuracy counts as classified.

assertions.value: The authors state that a locally-easy dataset is a necessary condition for the optimization curve to lie within the low-bodyness subspace but not a sufficient one, because initial points may exist that connect to the global minima only through paths that leave the subspace.
quotes: Evidently, having a locally-easy dataset is a necessary condition for the optimization curve to lie within the lowbodyness subspace, but it is nonetheless not a sufficient one.
It is entirely possible that there exist initial points that are only connected to the global minima through paths
that need to leave the subspace.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their own framework in Section III.B.

assertions.value: The authors state that Result 1 is only an average statement that holds for randomly initialized QCNNs, that it gives no practical means to simulate the QCNN during training, and that their numerical simulations are a heuristic extension that should not be considered a bridge between average-case and worst-case scenarios.
quotes: To finish, we note that the results in Result 1 are only an average statement, meaning that they only hold for randomly initialized QCNNs.

our numerical simulations are a heuristic extension of the classical average case simulability entailed by Result 1, and should not be considered a bridge between average-case and worstcase scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results of the companion Ref. [88] imply that randomly initialized QCNNs are classically simulable, but do not imply that the simulation is efficient or faithful throughout the whole training process, and that they do not imply that the regions of the landscape relevant during training can be simulated.

assertions.value: The authors define a model as classically simulable if a classical algorithm takes an efficient description of the problem plus the data obtained from quantum devices in an initial data acquisition phase and returns a loss estimate whose minimization leads to a simulated trained model capable of classification accuracies comparable to those of the original model.
quotes: we say that a model is classically simulable if there exists a classical algorithm A that takes as input an efficient description of the problem, as well as the data obtained from quantum devices in an initial data acquisition phase

assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of classical simulability adopted in Section II.B.
assertions.reader_inference: The definition asks only for comparable accuracy, not for the simulation to track the exact QCNN's trained parameters.

assertions.value: The authors say that if there is no need to run the parametrized quantum circuit on a quantum device, the QML model's information processing abilities can be considered dequantized, and that their approach is a substantial but not full dequantization because a state preparation and local Pauli measurement experiment may still be required.
quotes: if there is no need to run the parametrized quantum circuit on a quantum device, one can consider that the QML model’s information processing abilities are dequantized.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use only shallow embedding schemes, one and three layers for the hardware efficient and classically hard encodings, because deep versions are not useful and can give states too entangled for the QCNN's trainability guarantees, and that as a direct consequence all data encoded states admit an efficient MPS decomposition.

as it is well known that deep versions of these encoding are not useful [123]
A direct consequence of this fact is that all data encoded states will all admit an efficient MPS decomposition.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement, resting on Ref. [123] for the claim about deep embeddings.
assertions.reader_inference: This restricts the classical-data result to shallow encodings; the paper does not test deep encodings.

assertions.value: The authors state that all of the QML models used for the classical datasets are fully classically simulable because the embedding scheme itself is classically simulable, so no quantum resources appear to be needed, and that using QCNN-based QML schemes for classical data appears to be an ill-motivated task.
quotes: all of the QML models used here are fully classically simulable
As such, it appears that no quantum resources are needed to simulate the QCNN.
using QCNN-based QML schemes for classical data appears to be an ill-motivated task.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, resting on Ref. [123] and on the shallow embeddings used.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion holds for the shallow encodings and the four image datasets tested here.

assertions.value: The authors report that a random forest classified the two phases of 500 ground states of the n = 100 qubit XXX bond-alternating model, using overlaps with all single-nontrivial-Pauli strings plus 500 two-nontrivial-operator strings as features, 350 training states and 150 test states averaged over 200 trainings, with 100% accuracy, and they conclude the dataset is locally easy.
quotes: We generate 500 ground states from an n = 100 qubit XXX Bond Alternating model via DMRG
plus 500 operators containing two non-trivial operators
We use 350 states for training (evenly split between phases and randomly distributed within each phase) and 150 states for testing.
Finally, we average the predicted labels over 200 independent trainings.
As clearly observed in Fig. 12, the classification achieves 100% accuracy.
This result, entirely independent of the QCNN, demonstrates the intrinsic features of the datasets, making them easily classifiable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The features are overlaps of the DMRG ground states, which read as exact expectation values rather than shadow estimates. The phases are far apart in J2 (0 to 1 against 1 to 2), and the text does not say whether states close to the transition were included.

assertions.value: The authors report, on an enlarged dataset of 500 samples with 400 used for training, that the number of shadows needed for successful classification increases sublinearly with system size for the XXX model and appears independent of system size for the Haldane model, and they note that further tuning could change the XXX dependence.
quotes: Here, we enlarge the dataset to 500 samples, out of which 400 are employed in the training stage.

The number of shadows to perform successful classification in the XXX model increases sublinearly with system size, while there it seems to be independent of the system size in the case of the Haldane model.

However, it is also possible that further hyper-tuning of the model (preselection of relevant Pauli strings, increase in number of iterations, etc.) lead to a classification process which barely depends on system size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, read from heat maps in Figures 10 and 11.
assertions.reader_inference: The main text calls the dataset 100 samples with up to 75 for training; Appendix C changes both numbers, so the scaling study is not the same experiment as the main text.

assertions.value: The authors state that no overfitting seems to be taking place in the optimization, because raising the number of training points leaves the number of shadows needed for classification almost unchanged.

assertions.reader_inference: No held-out gap or learning curve is shown in the text to support the inference.

instead of numerically evaluating all coefficients cα during the Pauli Propagation, we only store a graphical representation of the splitting and merging of Pauli paths during an
we choose a truncation threshold k, and if a Pauli operator crosses this threshold at any part of the
we employ a so-called frequency truncation which affects the coefficients cα(θ).
We can estimate the variance of the coefficients cβ,s across the dataset (potentially inside the sliding window) and only evaluate along the paths with high variance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own algorithm in Appendix B.1.

assertions.reader_inference: The sliding window and the variance selection both use knowledge of the dataset's geometry and labels, which narrows how far the result transfers to unstructured data.

assertions.value: The authors state that applying a Pauli gate to a Pauli operator either leaves it unchanged or creates two different Pauli operators, so that simulating a circuit without truncation can create a number of Pauli operators exponential in the number of gates.
quotes: This implies that simulating such a quantum circuit can create a number of Pauli operators that is exponential in the number of gates m.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard property of Pauli propagation; the derivation of Eq. (B6) precedes the statement.

assertions.value: The authors describe their tensor network method as three steps: keep only low-bodyness information of the input data, find the optimal classifying operator as an MPS in the low-bodyness operator subspace, and lastly compile the circuit ansatz so its Heisenberg-evolved measurement operator is close to that operator, the last step being optional for the classification task and needed to find the ansatz parameters.
quotes: Then, we solve the binary classification task by finding the optimal classifying operator as represented by an MPS in the low-bodyness operator subspace.
Lastly, we compile the quantum circuit ansatz at hand such that the Heisenberg evolved measurement operator is as close as possible to the one found at the previous step.
which is optional with respect to the classification task, but which is needed
to find the optimal parameters of the circuital ansatz we started with.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own method in Appendix B.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Because step three is optional, the classical-dataset accuracies in Table I can come from the optimal low-bodyness operator found in step two; the text does not say whether a compiled QCNN with actual circuit parameters reached those accuracies, so the match to a QCNN with realizable parameters is not shown there.

assertions.value: The authors state that the constrained bodyness tensor network method currently applies only to binary classification tasks, fares best with one-dimensional quantum systems, and leaves multi-class problems and higher dimensional topologies to future work.
quotes: This method is currently applicable to binary classification tasks and fares best with one-dimensional quantum systems, we leave for future work the extension to multi-class problems and higher dimensional topologies.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their method in Appendix B.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the constraint on the evolved measurement operator to the low-bodyness subspace reproduces the behavior of an average QCNN under random initialization and proves sufficient to solve the task at hand, and that for a one-dimensional QCNN with logarithmically many layers the tensor network representation cannot raise the bond dimension by an exponential amount, so the full simulation and compilation is always efficient.
quotes: This constraint reproduces the behavior of an average QCNN under
random initialization, and proves to be sufficient to solve the task at hand.
increase the bond dimension of the MPS it acts on by an exponential (in the number of qubits n) amount. Hence the
full simulation and compilation of the QCNN is always efficient.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argument stated by the authors without a bound on the polynomial degree.
assertions.reader_inference: The efficiency claim gives no explicit bond dimension bound for the compilation step for Table I; Appendix E gives a measured bond dimension only for a different (measurement-based) example.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for a measurement-based QCNN evolving a random product state with Haar random convolution gates and random control unitaries, for system sizes n equal to 2 to the power m with m from 3 to 10, the maximum MPS bond dimension grows at most proportionally to n (the text layer prints it as chi, tilde, n and a trailing digit on separate lines), so the MPS simulation cost scales polynomially in n, as n cubed.
quotes: In this example, the initial state is a random product state, and the unitaries forming
by the SVD performed after applying each gate, the total cost scales as O(n3), i.e., polynomially in n.
Results are shown for n = 2m for m = 3, 4, . . . , 10.
All unitaries in the convolutional layer, as well as the control unitaries, were randomly sampled from U(4) and U(2), respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on random circuits; the scaling formula is garbled in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The bond dimension is read as n over 8, which is consistent with the later extrapolation of 4096 to 32,768 qubits (4096 times 8). This example has no classification task or training: it is a bond-dimension study on random inputs and random gates, so no classification accuracy for measurement-based QCNNs appears in the text I read, although Section III says the simpler tracing out QCNNs achieve similar or better success than measurement-based ones.

assertions.value: The authors state that state-of-the-art MPS methods on a laptop allow bond dimension up to about 4096, so that a laptop could simulate a measurement-based QCNN of up to 32,768 qubits, while noting that even modest polynomial scaling can quickly become intractable in practice and that they expect smaller bond dimensions in a typical training process than for random gates.
quotes: it is worth mentioning that in practice even modest polynomial scaling can quickly become intractable.

However, state-of-the-art methods allow MPS simulations on a laptop with bond dimension up to χ ∼ 4096, meaning that a laptop could simulate a QCNN with up to 32,768 qubits, far beyond the capabilities of current quantum computers.
whereas in practice one would expect smaller values of χ during a typical training process.
assertions.certainty_reason: Extrapolation by the authors from a bond dimension limit, not run.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls random gates the worst-case scenario, while Section III.A says random initialization is the average case; the two descriptions do not agree.

assertions.value: The authors state that using measurement outcomes for feed-forward operations precludes Heisenberg-evolution techniques such as LOWESA and other Pauli propagation, so measurement-based QCNNs are simulated with classical shadows and tensor networks instead, which work because measurements destroy entanglement and Pauli shadows give separable product states.
quotes: that the fact that we use measurement information for feed-forward operations precludes the use of Heisenberg-evolution
type techniques such as LOWESA or other Pauli propagation techniques.
this combination actually enables efficient simulation vis standard MPS techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state which of their methods do not apply to measurement-based QCNNs in Appendix E.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two instantiations they simulate, one-dimensional tracing out and measurement-based QCNNs, are the easiest to simulate classically, that QCNNs in two or more dimensions or with more exotic topologies would raise the simulation cost and were not pursued because such architectures have not been explored, and that they leave the burden of proof to practitioners.
quotes: it is clear that these are the easiest to classically simulate.
Clearly, this would increase the simulation cost, potentially making it prohibitively expensive even at modest sizes.
In this work, we decided not to pursue this route as these QCNNs architectures have not been explored, and are not known to be useful in cases where simple one-dimensional ones fail.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their architectures in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that non-classically simulable datasets and QCNNs can readily be constructed by embedding Shor's algorithm or a cryptographic assumption into the problem, but that these are usually mathematical artifacts far from realistic practical problems, and that their results do not exclude examples where the QCNN needs to leave the classically simulable regime.
quotes: one can readily construct nonclassically simulable datasets and QCNNs by embedding Shor’s algorithm or some cryptographic assumption into the problem
but these are usually mathematical artifacts that are nowhere near related to realistic practical problems.
this does not mean that examples could exist where the QCNN needs to leave the classically simulable regime to solve a given task.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their claim in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that obtaining classical shadows needs only state preparation and single qubit measurements, which are substantially easier than running the QCNN on quantum hardware, so that a universal digital quantum computer may no longer be required, and that for quantum input data a quantum computer is still needed to obtain the shadows.
quotes: Fundamentally, at least for the case of quantum input data, a quantum computer is needed to obtain classical shadows.

the resource requirements (state preparation and then single qubit measurements) are substantially easier than running the QCNN on quantum hardware - so much easier that a universal digital quantum computer may no longer be required.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' judgment; no resource count for the shadows experiment on hardware is given.

assertions.value: The authors propose a setting of classical training and quantum deployment, in which a QCNN is trained on a classical device via classical shadows and the optimal parameters are then used on a quantum computer for new data, and they state that whether classical simulation is efficient compared with training on a quantum computer is left as an open question.
quotes: Another positive spin of our results is a possible setting of “classical training and quantum deployment”
We also leave this open as a future research question.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal by the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they strongly believe the techniques can serve as blueprints to classically simulate other quantum neural network architectures composed of local parametrized gates, and that whether good enough solutions exist within the low-bodyness subspace for those architectures is an open question needing case-by-case direct simulation.
quotes: We strongly believe that the techniques introduced here can serve as blueprints to classi-
Whether there exists good enough solutions within such subspace as they do for QCNNs is an open question which will likely require a case-by-case analysis via direct simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A belief stated by the authors, with the open question named as untested.

assertions.value: The authors state that whether the use of trivial datasets in QML benchmarking is a positive bias effect, where only successful QCNN trainings are published, or an underlying phenomenon of physical problems, is left as an open question.
quotes: Whether the fact that we use trivial datasets in our QML model benchmarking is a positive bias effect (i.e., only successful QCNN trainings make it into the published literature) or a more underlying phenomenon of physical problems is left as an open question.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors name an open question in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that the heuristic success of QCNNs relates to two facts, that randomly initialized QCNNs operate only on low-bodyness information of their input states and that QCNNs are commonly benchmarked on locally-easy datasets, and that models could be showing heuristic success only because they are benchmarked on simple problems whose action can be classically simulated.
quotes: we relate their heuristic success to two facts.
Models could only be showing heuristic success because they are benchmarked on simple problems, for which their action can be classically simulated.
This insight points to the fact that non-trivial datasets are a truly necessary ingredient for moving forward with QML.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' causal interpretation of their results.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper shows the surrogate works on the datasets tested; it does not test the causal claim that QCNN success comes from the dataset simplicity, for example by finding a dataset where the QCNN fails and a deeper one succeeds.

assertions.value: The authors argue that until the viability of tracing out and measurement-based QCNNs on interesting non-trivial datasets can be demonstrated there is no reason to believe QCNNs will be useful, and present non-trivial datasets as a challenge to the community.
quotes: until the viability of tracing out- and measurement-based QCNNs for such datasets can be demonstrated there is no reason to believe QCNNs will be useful.
the field of QML is in dire need of interesting, non-trivial datasets
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' position.

assertions.value: The authors state that they compiled classical and quantum datasets used in the literature to benchmark QCNNs and heuristically show that they are all locally-easy and that the classification task can be solved while remaining in the low-bodyness subspace, and that their simulations show classical emulation for essentially all datasets used in the literature.
assertions.anchor: Section III.B, p6; Section IV, p7
quotes: we compiled classical and quantum datasets used in the literature to benchmark QCNNs, and we heuristically show not only that they are all locally-easy
its information processing capabilities can be emulated by classical computers for essentially all datasets used in the literature
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary claim over the datasets they tested.
assertions.reader_inference: The tested set is four quantum model families and four image datasets; the compilation of the literature's datasets is not listed beyond those, so all datasets in the literature is an extrapolation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their finite sample shadow-based simulations can outperform full QCNNs trained with no finite sampling.
quotes: we show that our finite sample shadow-based simulations can outperform full QCNNs trained with no finite sampling.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim; the comparison is against literature numbers.
assertions.reader_inference: No full QCNN was trained in this paper, so the comparison is with accuracies the authors cite from other work.
